Reversed only the zero from $(x+6)$: this factor is zero at $x=-6$, not $x=6$.
Missed the third factor — a factored cubic has three zeroes here, one per factor.
Made a sign error in $(-4)(3)(-2)$; the two negative constants multiply to a positive.
Added the constants, $-4+3-2=-3$, instead of multiplying them.
Used only the constant of the first factor instead of multiplying all three constants.
Ignored the $-x$ in the factor $(1-x)$, taking its highest-power term as $+x$.
Multiplied the constant terms $(-2)(5)(1)=-10$ instead of the coefficients of $x$.
Multiplied the constant terms as $2 \times 5 \times 1 = 10$, dropping the minus sign in $(3x-2)$.
Read the falling right end as a positive leading coefficient; a falling right end requires a negative leading coefficient.
Read ends pointing in the same direction as odd degree; odd-degree polynomials have ends in opposite directions.
Reversed both rules: the falling right end indicates a negative leading coefficient, and the matching end directions indicate even degree.

questions.solution_text: The right end falls, so the leading coefficient is negative. Both ends point down, so the degree is even.

options.why: Used a negative leading coefficient, which makes the right end fall instead of rise.
Dropped the factor $x$, losing the zero at the origin and giving a quadratic instead of a cubic.
Read the left zero as $-3$ instead of $-2$.

questions.solution_text: The zeroes are $-2$, $0$ and $2$, so the factors are $(x+2)$, $x$ and $(x-2)$. The leading coefficient is $1$, so $y=x(x-2)(x+2)$.

questions.question_text: Which monic cubic polynomial has zeroes $x=-2$, $x=3$ and $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$?

options.why: Kept each zero's sign in its factor instead of using $(x-a)$ for a zero at $x=a$.
Used $7$ instead of $\frac{7}{2}$ for the third zero.
Found the correct zeroes but used leading coefficient $2$, so the polynomial is not monic.

questions.solution_text: A zero at $x=a$ gives the factor $(x-a)$. Using three factors with leading coefficient $1$ gives the monic polynomial $P(x)=(x+2)(x-3)(x-\dfrac{7}{2})$.

questions.question_text: By factorising, find the zeroes of $y=x^{3}-25x$.

options.why: Forgot that the common factor $x$ also gives a zero at the origin.
Stopped at $x(x^{2}-25)$ and set $x^{2}=25$ without taking the square root correctly.
Factorised the difference of squares but kept only the positive root of $x^{2}=25$.
Sign slip in $(-1)(2)(4)(-6)$ — the two negative constants multiply to a positive.
Added the constants of the factors instead of multiplying them.
Assumed a quartic has constant term $0$; here none of the factors has constant term $0$.
Dropped the negative sign in the multiplier, giving $y=24$ at $x=0$ and a rising right end.
Reversed the signs of all three zeroes when writing the factors.
Used multiplier $-1$ without checking the given point; this gives $y=-12$ at $x=0$, not $-24$.

questions.solution_text: The zeroes give $y=k(x+3)(x-1)(x-4)$. Use the $y$-intercept: $-24=k(3)(-1)(-4)=12k$, so $k=-2$. Hence $y=-2(x+3)(x-1)(x-4)$.
